title: Dynamical observations and finite system realization

items.title: Discrete linear input-state-output experiments
items.statement:
Let $d\ge0$, $m,p\ge1$, and $q\ge1$ be integers, and let $h>0$ be a fixed
sampling interval. A real **discrete linear input-state-output experiment** of
state dimension $d$, input dimension $m$, output dimension $p$, and horizon
$q$ consists of matrices $A\in M_{d\times d}(\mathbb R)$,
$B\in M_{d\times m}(\mathbb R)$, and $C\in M_{p\times d}(\mathbb R)$, an
initial state $x_0\in\mathbb R^d$, and known inputs
$(u_k)_{0\le k<q-1}$ in $\mathbb R^m$. The states are defined by
$$x_{k+1}=Ax_k+Bu_k\qquad(0\le k<q-1),$$
and the exact sampled outputs at times $kh$ are $y_k=Cx_k$ for
$0\le k<q$. When observations are perturbed, the observed outputs are
$\widetilde y_k=y_k+\eta_k$ for deterministic error vectors
$\eta_k\in\mathbb R^p$; the exact-data convention is $\eta_k=0$ for all $k$.
No probability law is assigned to the errors. A numerical or discretization
error that changes the forward map is distinct from this additive observation
error.

For an impulse-response experiment with zero initial state, first input
$u_0=v\in\mathbb R^m$, and later inputs zero, the **Markov parameters** are
$$M_k:=CA^kB\in M_{p\times m}(\mathbb R)\qquad(k\ge0),$$
so the output one sample after the impulse is $y_{k+1}=M_kv$. Matrix powers
use $A^0=I_d$ and $A^{k+1}=A^kA$. If $d=0$, the state space consists of its
single zero vector and the matrices have the corresponding empty shapes.
items.strategy: Specify the state, input, output, time-indexing, noise, and impulse-response conventions directly in finite-dimensional coordinates.

items.title: Exact block-Hankel realization
items.statement:
Fix integers $d\ge0$, $m,p\ge1$, and $q\ge1$. The input is a list of exact
Markov matrices
$$M_0,\ldots,M_{2q-1}\in M_{p\times m}(\mathbb R).$$
Use the exact-real linear-algebra model: an exact rank test returns the rank of
a finite real matrix; a thin rank-$d$ singular-value decomposition of a
rank-$d$ matrix $H_0$ returns $H_0=U_d\Sigma_dV_d^{\mathsf T}$ with
$\Sigma_d$ diagonal and strictly positive, and an exact Moore--Penrose routine
returns a matrix satisfying the four Penrose equations. A routine failure or a
returned object that fails its stated exact identities is reported explicitly.
This specification makes no finite-bit computability or complexity claim for
arbitrary real inputs.

Form the $q$-by-$q$ block Hankel matrices
$$H_0=[M_{i+j}]_{0\le i,j<q},\qquad H_1=[M_{i+j+1}]_{0\le i,j<q},$$
each of shape $qp$ by $qm$. Execute the following steps.

1. Apply the exact rank test to $H_0$. If it fails, return
   `failed-solve`; if its value is not $d$, return `inconsistent-rank-data`.

2. If $d=0$, use the empty factorization $H_0=\widehat O\widehat R$ with
   $\widehat O$ of shape $qp$ by $0$ and $\widehat R$ of shape $0$ by $qm$.
   If $d>0$, obtain the thin rank-$d$ SVD in the declared exact model and set
   $$\widehat O:=U_d\Sigma_d^{1/2},\qquad \widehat R:=\Sigma_d^{1/2}V_d^{\mathsf T}.$$
   Verify $H_0=\widehat O\widehat R$, $\operatorname{rank}\widehat O=d$,
   and $\operatorname{rank}\widehat R=d$; if any operation or verification
   fails, return `failed-solve`.

3. Compute the exact Moore--Penrose inverses $\widehat O^+$ and
   $\widehat R^+$ and verify their four Penrose equations. If a computation or
   verification fails, return `failed-solve`.

4. Set $\widehat A:=\widehat O^+H_1\widehat R^+$, let $\widehat B$ be the first $m$ columns of $\widehat R$, and let $\widehat C$ be the first $p$ rows of $\widehat O$. Return `success` with $(\widehat A,\widehat B,\widehat C)$. For $d=0$,
   these are the corresponding empty matrices.

The routine can report `failed-solve` for a failed or invalid exact-operation
backend. The existence theorems for finite-matrix SVDs and Moore--Penrose
inverses ensure that the exact mathematical operations requested in steps 2–3
exist; this definition alone asserts no noisy rank selection or stable
parameter recovery.
items.strategy: Build the two q-by-q block Hankel matrices from M_0,...,M_{2q-1}; use a rank-d thin-SVD factorization and unique finite-matrix Moore-Penrose inverses, with explicit rank and solve checks.

items.title: Finite observability identifies the initial state
items.statement:
Let $d\ge0$, $m,p\ge1$, and $q\ge1$ be integers,
and consider a real discrete input-state-output experiment with known matrices
$A,B,C$, known inputs $u_0,\ldots,u_{q-2}$, and unknown initial state $x_0$. For
$0\le k<q$, set
$$f_0:=0,\qquad f_k:=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}CA^{k-1-j}Bu_j\quad(k\ge1),$$
and define the finite observability matrix $$O_q:=\begin{bmatrix}C\\CA\\ \vdots\\CA^{q-1}\end{bmatrix}.$$ The corrected noiseless output stack is $$z:=\begin{bmatrix}y_0-f_0\\y_1-f_1\\ \vdots\\y_{q-1}-f_{q-1}\end{bmatrix}=O_qx_0.$$
The map $x_0\mapsto z$ is injective if and only if
$\operatorname{rank}O_q=d$. If $d=0$, both injectivity and the rank condition
hold for the singleton state space. If $d\ge1$ and $O_q$ has full column rank,
let $\sigma_{\min}(O_q)>0$ be its least singular value. For any additive stacked
observation error $e\in\mathbb R^{qp}$, the minimum-norm least-squares estimate
of $x_0$ from $z+e$ is $\widehat x_0=O_q^+(z+e)$, and it satisfies
$$\|\widehat x_0-x_0\|_2\le\frac{\|e\|_2}{\sigma_{\min}(O_q)}.$$
items.strategy: Expand the recurrence to isolate O_q x_0, characterize injectivity by its kernel and rank-nullity, and derive the least-squares perturbation bound from the singular values and orthogonal projection properties of the Moore-Penrose inverse.

items.title: State similarity preserves input-output data
items.statement:
Let $d\ge0$, $m,p\ge1$, and $q\ge1$ be integers. Suppose a noiseless
experiment has matrices $A\in M_{d\times d}(\mathbb R)$,
$B\in M_{d\times m}(\mathbb R)$, and $C\in M_{p\times d}(\mathbb R)$,
initial state $x_0\in\mathbb R^d$, and common inputs
$(u_k)_{0\le k<q-1}$. For any invertible $T\in M_d(\mathbb R)$ define
$$\widehat A=T^{-1}AT,\qquad \widehat B=T^{-1}B,\qquad \widehat C=CT,\qquad \widehat x_0=T^{-1}x_0.$$
The experiment with $(\widehat A,\widehat B,\widehat C,\widehat x_0)$ and the
same inputs has the same output $y_k$ at every sample $0\le k<q$. The equality
holds for every horizon and every common input sequence.
items.strategy: Prove by induction that the transformed state at each sample is T^{-1} times the original state, then substitute in the output equation.

items.title: Hankel realization recovers a controllable and observable system
items.statement:
Let $d\ge0$, $m,p\ge1$, and $q\ge1$ be integers,
and let $A\in M_{d\times d}(\mathbb R)$,
$B\in M_{d\times m}(\mathbb R)$, and $C\in M_{p\times d}(\mathbb R)$ define
a discrete linear input-state-output experiment. Let
$$M_k:=CA^kB\qquad(0\le k\le2q-1),$$
$$O_q:=\begin{bmatrix}C\\CA\\ \vdots\\CA^{q-1}\end{bmatrix},\qquad R_q:=\begin{bmatrix}B&AB&\cdots&A^{q-1}B\end{bmatrix}.$$
Assume $\operatorname{rank}O_q=\operatorname{rank}R_q=d$, the finite-horizon
observability and controllability conditions. Assume that every exact rank,
SVD, and Moore--Penrose call made by the block-Hankel realization algorithm
completes and passes its stated exact checks. Then the algorithm returns
`success` with matrices $(\widehat A,\widehat B,\widehat C)$, and there is an
invertible $T\in M_d(\mathbb R)$ such that
$$\widehat A=T^{-1}AT,\qquad \widehat B=T^{-1}B,\qquad \widehat C=CT.$$
For $d=0$, this means the unique zero-dimensional realization and the unique
invertible map on the zero space.
items.strategy: Show H_0=O_qR_q and H_1=O_qAR_q, match the full-rank SVD factors to O_q and R_q by one invertible coordinate change, then use the Moore-Penrose left/right inverse identities.

title: Dynamical observations and finite system realization — Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Continuous-time frequencies alias under fixed discrete sampling
items.statement:
For a fixed sampling interval $h>0$, if a real continuous-time signal has the
form $y_\omega(t)=\cos(\omega t)$ for an unknown frequency $\omega\ge0$, then
its entire noiseless sample sequence $(y_\omega(kh))_{k\in\mathbb N_0}$
uniquely determines $\omega$.
items.strategy: Compare the cosine outputs at frequencies 0 and 2 pi/h and use the 2 pi-periodicity of sine and cosine at every integer sample index.
items.axiom_use: No choice principle is used; the sample identities are finite trigonometric equalities.

items.title: Two similar realizations with identical data
items.statement:
Let
$$A=\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix},\quad B=\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix},\quad C=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\end{bmatrix},\quad x_0=\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix},\quad T=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix},\quad T^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}1&-1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}.$$
The transformed realization has
$$\widehat A=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\0&1\end{bmatrix},\quad \widehat B=\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix},\quad \widehat C=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\end{bmatrix},\quad \widehat x_0=\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}.$$
The two state-space descriptions differ, but for every common input sequence
their exact output sequences agree at every sample.
items.strategy: Choose an explicit nonsingular triangular coordinate change, compute the transformed matrices and initial state, and invoke the similarity theorem.

items.title: An unobserved state mode
items.statement:
Take $d=2$, one input, one output, $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&2\end{bmatrix}$,
$B=0_{2\times1}$, and $C=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\end{bmatrix}$. For every finite
horizon $q\ge1$ with zero inputs, the distinct initial states
$x_0=(0,0)^{\mathsf T}$ and $x'_0=(0,1)^{\mathsf T}$ produce the same exact
output sequence, namely $y_k=0$ for all $0\le k<q$. The finite observability
matrix has rank $1<2$.
items.strategy: Compute the output difference from the second basis state and show C A^k e_2=0 for every k.

items.title: Forward Euler creates an observation-map error
items.statement:
For each parameter $\theta\in\mathbb R$, solve
$$\dot z_\theta(t)=\theta t,\qquad z_\theta(0)=0\qquad(0\le t\le1),$$
and observe $z_\theta(1)$. The exact observation map is
$A(\theta)=\theta/2$. Apply one explicit forward-Euler step of size $h=1$,
$$z_1=z_0+h\theta t_0\quad\text{with }(t_0,z_0)=(0,0);$$
the resulting discretized observation map is $A_h(\theta)=0$. In the computed
inversion error budget with $X=Y=\mathbb R$, truth $\theta=1$, zero observation
error, and $\lambda=1$, the pre-inversion discrepancy is $d_h=1/2$.
items.strategy: Verify the polynomial ODE solution, compute the one-step Euler map, and check that the resulting scalar forward maps satisfy the hypotheses of the computed-inversion error budget.
items.axiom_use: No choice principle is used; the ODE solution and scalar operator checks are explicit.

items.title: A small Hankel singular value amplifies a realization perturbation
items.statement:
Use the exact block-Hankel realization procedure with $q=d=m=p=1$, and assume
that every exact rank, SVD, and Moore--Penrose call made in both runs completes
and passes its stated exact checks. For any $0<\varepsilon\le1$, the scalar system
$A=0$, $B=\varepsilon$, $C=1$ has Markov data $M_0=\varepsilon$ and
$M_1=0$, and $H_0=[\varepsilon]$ has singular value $\varepsilon$. The exact
algorithm returns $\widehat A=0$. If only $M_1$ is perturbed to
$\widetilde M_1=\sqrt\varepsilon$, the pair $(M_0,\widetilde M_1)$ is itself
generated by the scalar system $\widetilde A=1/\sqrt\varepsilon$,
$\widetilde B=\varepsilon$, $\widetilde C=1$, so the exact algorithm returns
$\widetilde A$. Thus an absolute Markov-data perturbation $\sqrt\varepsilon$
can change the recovered transition value by $1/\sqrt\varepsilon$.
items.strategy: Evaluate the q=1 Hankel matrices and the exact algorithm for a one-state system and for the perturbed two-parameter data, then compare the recovered transition values.
items.axiom_use: No choice principle is used; the example is a finite scalar calculation.
